[LLM] Burst AWS API calls fanned across Cloudflare Workers egress (104.28.0.0/16) for one principal Command & Control High
Detects the LLM-agent evasion fingerprint Sysdig described: 10+ AWS API calls from one IAM principal/role within a sub-minute window, originating from many distinct IPs inside the Cloudflare Workers CIDR. This breaks per-source-IP correlation and is unlike legitimate Cloudflare-Workers-backed workloads which typically use a stable role and steady cadence. Rationale: Article: 12 AWS API calls fanned across 11 distinct Cloudflare Workers IPs in 22 seconds for the same principal. The 5-distinct-IPs-and-10-calls-in-2-minutes shape directly mirrors that burst while staying comfortably above any single-app Cloudflare-Workers usage pattern. CIDR + same-principal aggregation is the key — neither alone is high-fidelity.
ATT&CKT1090.003 T1078.004
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
source:cloudtrail CIDR(@network.client.ip, 104.28.0.0/16) NOT @userIdentity.type:AWSService
# log group: /aws/cloudtrail
fields @timestamp, eventName, eventSource, sourceIPAddress, userIdentity.arn, userIdentity.type, userIdentity.sessionContext.sessionIssuer.userName
| filter sourceIPAddress like /^104\.28\./
      and userIdentity.type != "AWSService"
| stats count(*) as api_calls, count_distinct(sourceIPAddress) as src_ips, count_distinct(eventName) as distinct_apis, latest(eventName) as last_event by userIdentity.arn, bin(2m)
| filter api_calls >= 10 and src_ips >= 5
| sort api_calls desc
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count from datamodel=Change where All_Changes.vendor_product="AWS CloudTrail" by All_Changes.user, All_Changes.src, All_Changes.action, _time span=2m | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Changes)` | where cidrmatch("104.28.0.0/16", src) | stats dc(src) as distinct_src_ips, dc(action) as distinct_actions, sum(count) as api_calls, values(src) as src_ips, values(action) as actions by user, _time | where distinct_src_ips >= 5 AND api_calls >= 10
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Change where All_Changes.vendor_product="AWS CloudTrail" by All_Changes.user, All_Changes.src, All_Changes.action, _time span=2m | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Changes)` | where cidrmatch("104.28.0.0/16", src) | stats dc(src) as distinct_src_ips, dc(action) as distinct_actions, sum(count) as api_calls, values(src) as src_ips, values(action) as actions by user, _time | where distinct_src_ips >= 5 AND api_calls >= 10
[LLM] AWS Secrets Manager retrieval from Cloudflare Workers egress pool Actions on Objectives High
Detects ListSecrets / GetSecretValue CloudTrail events originating from the 104.28.0.0/16 Cloudflare Workers CIDR. In the Sysdig intrusion this exact pair retrieved the SSH private key the agent used to pivot to the bastion — the source-IP-vs-Secrets-Manager combination is the high-fidelity signal. Rationale: Article: AWS Secrets Manager call retrieved an SSH private key, source IP 104.28.0.0/16. Pairing eventSource secretsmanager.amazonaws.com with the Cloudflare Workers CIDR is the article's exact fingerprint — sub-second decision, single CloudTrail line.
ATT&CKT1552.005 T1555.006
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
title: AWS Secrets Manager Retrieval From Cloudflare Workers Egress Pool
id: b2c3d4e5-f6a7-4801-bcde-f23456789012
description: Detects AWS Secrets Manager retrieval calls originating from the 104.28.0.0/16 Cloudflare Workers CIDR used by the LLM-agent intrusion to grab an SSH key.
references:
  - https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-use-llm-agent-to-move-from-marimo-rce/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/28
tags:
  - attack.credential_access
  - attack.t1555.006
logsource:
  product: aws
  service: cloudtrail
detection:
  selection:
    eventSource: 'secretsmanager.amazonaws.com'
    eventName:
      - 'GetSecretValue'
      - 'ListSecrets'
    sourceIPAddress|startswith: '104.28.'
  condition: selection
falsepositives:
  - Customer-owned Cloudflare Worker that legitimately retrieves secrets via the AWS SDK (allowlist by principal ARN)
level: high
source:cloudtrail @evt.name:(GetSecretValue OR ListSecrets) CIDR(@network.client.ip, 104.28.0.0/16)
# log group: /aws/cloudtrail
fields @timestamp, eventName, sourceIPAddress, userIdentity.arn, userIdentity.type, requestParameters.SecretId, requestParameters.Filters
| filter eventSource = "secretsmanager.amazonaws.com"
      and eventName in ["GetSecretValue", "ListSecrets"]
      and sourceIPAddress like /^104\.28\./
      and not isPresent(errorCode)
| sort @timestamp desc
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count from datamodel=Change where All_Changes.vendor_product="AWS CloudTrail" All_Changes.action IN ("GetSecretValue","ListSecrets") by All_Changes.user, All_Changes.src, All_Changes.action, All_Changes.object, _time | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Changes)` | where cidrmatch("104.28.0.0/16", src) | stats min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(action) as actions values(object) as secrets values(src) as src_ips count by user
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Change where All_Changes.vendor_product="AWS CloudTrail" All_Changes.action IN ("GetSecretValue","ListSecrets") by All_Changes.user, All_Changes.src, All_Changes.action, All_Changes.object, _time | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Changes)` | where cidrmatch("104.28.0.0/16", src) | stats min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(action) as actions values(object) as secrets values(src) as src_ips count by user
[LLM] SSH authentication to bastion from Cloudflare Workers CIDR (104.28.0.0/16) Actions on Objectives High
Detects successful SSH logons originating from the Cloudflare Workers egress pool, with multi-IP parallelism per user — the bastion-pivot stage Sysdig observed where eight parallel SSH sessions originated from six distinct CF Workers IPs against the same downstream bastion. Internal users virtually never authenticate to bastions via Cloudflare's CDN range. Rationale: Article: 8 SSH sessions came from 6 separate CF Workers IPs simultaneously against the bastion. Joining "successful sshd Accepted" with "src in 104.28.0.0/16" + the multi-IP-per-user aggregation hits the actual fan-out shape, not a generic CDN-IP false positive.
ATT&CKT1021.004 T1090.003
Data sourcesAuthentication
DeviceLogonEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "LogonSuccess"
| where Protocol == "Ssh" or InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "sshd"
| where ipv4_is_in_range(RemoteIP, "104.28.0.0/16")
| summarize SessionCount = count(), SrcIPs = make_set(RemoteIP), DistinctSrc = dcount(RemoteIP), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, AccountName, bin(Timestamp, 10m)
| where DistinctSrc >= 3 or SessionCount >= 5
| order by LastSeen desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ProcessName =~ "sshd"
| where SyslogMessage has "Accepted"
| extend SrcIP = extract(@"from\s+(\d+\.\d+\.\d+\.\d+)", 1, SyslogMessage), SshUser = extract(@"for\s+(\S+)\s+from", 1, SyslogMessage)
| where SrcIP startswith "104.28."
| summarize SessionCount = count(), SrcIPs = make_set(SrcIP), DistinctSrc = dcount(SrcIP), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by Computer, SshUser, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where DistinctSrc >= 3 or SessionCount >= 5
| order by LastSeen desc
source:linux.syslog @process.name:sshd "Accepted" CIDR(@network.client.ip, 104.28.0.0/16)
#event_simpleName=UserLogon
| RemoteAddressIP4=/^104\.28\./
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName], function={count() | distinct_count(RemoteAddressIP4, as=distinct_src) | min(_time, as=firstSeen) | max(_time, as=lastSeen)})
| distinct_src >= 3 OR _count >= 5
# log group: /aws/vpc/flowlogs
fields @timestamp, srcAddr, dstAddr, dstPort, action, bytes
| filter dstPort = 22 and action = "ACCEPT"
      and srcAddr like /^104\.28\./
| stats count(*) as flows, count_distinct(srcAddr) as src_ips, sum(bytes) as bytes_sent by dstAddr, bin(10m)
| filter src_ips >= 3 or flows >= 5
| sort @timestamp desc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.app=sshd Authentication.action=success by Authentication.src, Authentication.user, Authentication.dest, _time span=10m | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | where cidrmatch("104.28.0.0/16", src) | stats dc(src) as src_count sum(count) as session_count values(src) as src_ips by user, dest, bin_time | where src_count >= 3 OR session_count >= 5
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.app=sshd Authentication.action=success by Authentication.src, Authentication.user, Authentication.dest, _time span=10m | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | where cidrmatch("104.28.0.0/16", src) | stats dc(src) as src_count sum(count) as session_count values(src) as src_ips by user, dest, bin_time | where src_count >= 3 OR session_count >= 5
[LLM] PostgreSQL HEREDOC credential-table dump invoked from compromised host Actions on Objectives Medium
Detects psql being invoked with a HEREDOC and credential-table-targeting queries (users, credentials, password columns), often immediately preceded by a .pgpass read by the same user — the database exfiltration pattern Sysdig captured when the LLM agent enumerated the schema and immediately dumped a credential table that didn't even belong to the running application. Rationale: Article: agent read .pgpass, enumerated schema, and immediately dumped a credential table that doesn't belong to the running app, using HEREDOC-style structured commands. psql + (credential-table keywords OR `<<EOF` OR `COPY (`) is the article-specific intent; cross-correlating with a .pgpass read by the same account in the same window further sharpens it.
ATT&CKT1005 T1213 T1552.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
let PgpassReaders = DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where FileName == ".pgpass" or FolderPath endswith "/.pgpass"
    | where ActionType in ("FileOpenedForRead","FileCreated","FileModified")
    | project PgpassTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessId;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("psql","pg_dump")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(credentials|password|users|secrets|tokens|api_keys)"
   or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"<<\s*[A-Z_]+"
   or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)copy\s+\(?\s*select"
| join kind=leftouter PgpassReaders on DeviceId, $left.AccountName == $right.InitiatingProcessAccountName
| where isnotempty(PgpassTime) or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("credentials","users","<<")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, PgpassTime
| order by Timestamp desc
let PgpassReaders = ImFileEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where TargetFileName == ".pgpass" or TargetFilePath endswith "/.pgpass"
    | project PgpassTime = TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername;
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName in~ ("psql","pg_dump")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(credentials|password|users|secrets|tokens|api_keys)"
   or ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"<<\s*[A-Z_]+"
   or ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)copy\s+\(?\s*select"
| join kind=leftouter PgpassReaders on DvcHostname, $left.ActorUsername == $right.ActorUsername
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, PgpassTime
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: PostgreSQL Credential Table Dump via psql HEREDOC
id: c3d4e5f6-a7b8-4923-cdef-345678901234
description: Detects psql/pg_dump invocations consuming a HEREDOC and targeting credential or user tables — the database exfiltration step the LLM-agent intrusion executed against an internal PostgreSQL.
references:
  - https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-use-llm-agent-to-move-from-marimo-rce/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/28
tags:
  - attack.collection
  - attack.t1005
  - attack.exfiltration
  - attack.t1213
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: linux
detection:
  selection_proc:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/psql'
      - '/pg_dump'
  selection_intent:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'credentials'
      - 'users'
      - 'password'
      - 'secrets'
      - 'api_keys'
      - 'tokens'
      - '<<EOF'
      - 'COPY ('
  condition: selection_proc and selection_intent
falsepositives:
  - Application owners running ad-hoc COPY/SELECT against legitimate user tables
  - Backup jobs invoking pg_dump
level: medium
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.name:(psql OR pg_dump) @process.command_line:(*credentials* OR *password* OR *users* OR *secrets* OR *api_keys* OR *"<<EOF"* OR *"COPY ("*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\/(psql|pg_dump)$/i
| CommandLine=/(credentials|password|users|secrets|api_keys|tokens|<<\s*EOF|COPY\s*\()/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("psql","pg_dump") by host, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name, _time | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where match(process,"(?i)(credentials|password|users|secrets|tokens|api_keys)") OR match(process,"<<\s*[A-Z_]+") OR match(process,"(?i)copy\s+\(?\s*select") | join type=left host, user [| tstats summariesonly=true count as pgpass_reads from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name=".pgpass" by host, Filesystem.user | rename Filesystem.user as user | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`] | table _time host user process parent_process_name pgpass_reads
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("psql","pg_dump") by host, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name, _time | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where match(process,"(?i)(credentials|password|users|secrets|tokens|api_keys)") OR match(process,"<<\s*[A-Z_]+") OR match(process,"(?i)copy\s+\(?\s*select") | join type=left host, user [| tstats summariesonly=false count as pgpass_reads from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name=".pgpass" by host, Filesystem.user | rename Filesystem.user as user | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`] | table _time host user process parent_process_name pgpass_reads

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High

Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Less panic patching, more precision
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.

        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),

        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "5e6060df7e8114cb7b412260870efd1dc05979454bd907d8750c669ae6fcbcfe", "afc8a00883a4ea07df2dc1d4ed02f8a23b35c9456413b438a2d9ce3ae5076638", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "a2cf85d22a54e26794cbc7be16840bb1", "cc4d231df34e57f59eb970353c7d9de2") or SHA1 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "5e6060df7e8114cb7b412260870efd1dc05979454bd907d8750c669ae6fcbcfe", "afc8a00883a4ea07df2dc1d4ed02f8a23b35c9456413b438a2d9ce3ae5076638", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "a2cf85d22a54e26794cbc7be16840bb1", "cc4d231df34e57f59eb970353c7d9de2") or MD5 in~ ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "5e6060df7e8114cb7b412260870efd1dc05979454bd907d8750c669ae6fcbcfe", "afc8a00883a4ea07df2dc1d4ed02f8a23b35c9456413b438a2d9ce3ae5076638", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "a2cf85d22a54e26794cbc7be16840bb1", "cc4d231df34e57f59eb970353c7d9de2")

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "5e6060df7e8114cb7b412260870efd1dc05979454bd907d8750c669ae6fcbcfe", "afc8a00883a4ea07df2dc1d4ed02f8a23b35c9456413b438a2d9ce3ae5076638", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "a2cf85d22a54e26794cbc7be16840bb1", "cc4d231df34e57f59eb970353c7d9de2"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Critical

VaultJacking Attack Steals Entire Google Password Manager Vault With One Captured PIN

Cyber Security News
2026-05-28 8 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A new phishing technique called VaultJacking has emerged, and it is raising serious alarms across the cybersecurity community. With just a single captured 6-digit PIN, an attacker can walk away with an entire Google Password Manager vault, including every saved password and passkey stored inside. This is not a theoretical risk, as it is a [&#8230;] The post VaultJacking Attack Steals Entire Google Password Manager Vault With One Captured PIN appeared first on Cyber Security News .

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Browser navigation to Google Password Manager PIN prompt lookalike domain (VaultJacking phishing) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] New Google passkey / security key enrolled from unseen geo or IP (VaultJacking operator persistence)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations

[LLM] Browser navigation to Google Password Manager PIN prompt lookalike domain (VaultJacking phishing) Delivery Medium
Hunts the phishing prerequisite for VaultJacking: a user's browser visiting a non-google.com host that impersonates passwords.google.com / the GPM PIN prompt. VaultJacking is uniquely keyed on the 6-digit GPM PIN, so the phishing page mimics passwords.google.com / passkey-unlock surfaces rather than the standard accounts.google.com sign-in page — this is the differentiator from generic Google credential phishing. Rationale: Article (and corroborating gbhackers writeup) state the phishing page specifically mimics the Google Password Manager PIN prompt at passwords.google.com — a unique surface from generic accounts.google.com phishing. Hunting URL/hostname tokens that combine 'google' (or g00gle) with 'passwords'/'passkey'/'gpm'/'vault' targets the VaultJacking lure category specifically while excluding legitimate google.com traffic. Cross-checked: cybersecuritynews and gbhackers articles, MITRE T1566.002 / T1598.003. Cross-checked against: • https://gbhackers.com/google-password-vaults-via-single-pin/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/002/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1598/003/
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1598.003

[LLM] New Google passkey / security key enrolled from unseen geo or IP (VaultJacking operator persistence) Installation Medium
Detects the VaultJacking persistence step: after the GPM PIN is phished, the operator authenticates from their infrastructure and registers an operator-owned passkey on the victim's Google account, unlocking the synced vault. Pivots on new-passkey / new-2SV-device enrollment events in Google Workspace audit telemetry that originate from a country or IP the account has never used. Rationale: Article explicitly names this as the only outward-visible defender signal: 'train users to treat notifications like new passkey added or new sign-in on Windows as authentication events worth verifying every time.' The operator's passkey enrollment from their own infrastructure produces a new-device + new-geo signal in Google Workspace audit logs. Joining recent passkey-add events against a 30-day per-user IP/country baseline isolates the VaultJacking persistence step from genuine user enrollments. Cross-checked: gbhackers article confirms 'attackers register their own passkey on the victim's account to maintain persistence' and lists 'New passkey additions' + 'Device enrollment events in Google Workspace audit logs' as the recommended monitoring signals. Cross-checked against: • https://gbhackers.com/google-password-vaults-via-single-pin/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1098/001/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1556/
ATT&CKT1098.001 T1556 T1111
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes Authentication.Authentication
let LookbackDays = 30d;
let RecentHours = 24h;
let Baseline =
    CloudAppEvents
    | where Timestamp between (ago(LookbackDays) .. ago(RecentHours))
    | where Application has_any ("Google","GSuite","G Suite","Google Workspace")
    | summarize KnownCountries = make_set(CountryCode, 50),
                KnownIPs = make_set(IPAddress, 200),
                KnownUAs = make_set(UserAgent, 50)
            by AccountObjectId;
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(RecentHours)
| where Application has_any ("Google","GSuite","G Suite","Google Workspace")
| where ActionType has_any ("passkey","security_key","AddSecondFactor","TwoStepVerification","strong_authentication","webauthn","AddSecurityKey","register_credential")
    or ActivityType has_any ("passkey","security_key","device_register","Add device","Add second factor")
    or tostring(RawEventData) has_any ("registerPasskey","passkey_added","security_key_added","ENROLL_FOR_2SV","USE_STRONG_AUTHENTICATION","PASSKEY_CREATED")
| join kind=leftouter Baseline on AccountObjectId
| extend NewCountry = iff(isnotempty(CountryCode) and not(set_has_element(KnownCountries, CountryCode)), true, false),
         NewIP = iff(isnotempty(IPAddress) and not(set_has_element(KnownIPs, IPAddress)), true, false)
| where NewCountry or NewIP or isempty(KnownIPs)
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName,
          IPAddress, CountryCode, City, ISP, UserAgent,
          Application, ActionType, ActivityType,
          NewCountry, NewIP, ActivityObjects, RawEventData
| order by Timestamp desc

SecurityAlert
| where TimeGenerated > ago(RecentHours)
| where ProductName has_any ("Cloud App Security","Defender for Cloud Apps")
| where AlertName has_any ("passkey","security key","two-step","second factor","webauthn","strong authentication")
    or Description has_any ("passkey","security key","ENROLL_FOR_2SV","USE_STRONG_AUTHENTICATION","PASSKEY_CREATED")

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)

| order by conn_count desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

A malicious package named &#8220;mouse5212-super-formatter&#8221; was discovered on the npm registry, acting as an infostealer designed to quietly steal files from any developer who [&#8230;] The post AI-Generated npm Malware Accidentally Exposes Threat Actor’s Private GitHub Token appeared first on Cyber Security News .

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] npm install of malicious 'mouse5212-super-formatter' package · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Node.js exfiltration to GitHub Contents API following /mnt/user-data read · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Recursive enumeration of Anthropic Claude /mnt/user-data by node/npm process · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
[LLM] npm install of malicious 'mouse5212-super-formatter' package Delivery High
Detects developer or CI environments installing the OX-Security-flagged npm infostealer package by name. This is the entry point — catching the install kills the attack before /mnt/user-data is enumerated and exfiltrated. Rationale: Hardcoded on the OX Security-disclosed package name 'mouse5212-super-formatter' (676 downloads, still live on npm at publication). Pairs the package-name string with npm/node/yarn/pnpm process context to avoid the FP of someone just grepping/cat-ing the string in a doc. Corroborated by OX Security write-up, The Hacker News and The Register. Cross-checked against: • https://www.ox.security/blog/malware-slop-new-malicious-npm-package-leaks-its-own-github-private-token/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/malicious-npm-package-stole-files-from.html • https://www.theregister.com/cyber-crime/2026/05/27/supply-chain-brain-drain-npm-attacker-foolishly-leaks-own-github-private-token/5247424
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("npm","npm.exe","npm-cli.js","yarn","yarn.exe","pnpm","pnpm.exe","npx","npx.exe","node","node.exe")
     or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm","npm.exe","yarn","yarn.exe","pnpm","pnpm.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "mouse5212-super-formatter"
     or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "mouse5212-super-formatter"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, AccountName, AccountUpn, FolderPath, FileName,
          ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
  (SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where EventID == 4688
    | where NewProcessName endswith "\\npm.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\node.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\yarn.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\pnpm.exe"
    | where CommandLine has "mouse5212-super-formatter"
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName),
  (ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where ActingProcessName has_any ("npm","node","yarn","pnpm","npx")
         or ParentProcessName has_any ("npm","yarn","pnpm")
    | where ActingProcessCommandLine has "mouse5212-super-formatter" or TargetProcessCommandLine has "mouse5212-super-formatter"
    | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName),
  (Syslog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where Facility == "user" or ProcessName has_any ("npm","node","yarn","pnpm")
    | where SyslogMessage has "mouse5212-super-formatter"
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostName, ProcessName, SyslogMessage)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Recursive enumeration of Anthropic Claude /mnt/user-data by node/npm process Actions on Objectives Medium
Hunts node/npm/python processes that recursively read or stat large numbers of files under /mnt/user-data — the Anthropic Claude artifact directory that mouse5212-super-formatter walks before exfiltration. Catches both this campaign and copycats that target the same well-known AI-sandbox path. Rationale: Anchors on the specific /mnt/user-data path the OX Security report identifies as the recursive-walk target plus the JavaScript/Node runtime context of the npm package. Threshold of 5 unique files filters out single-file legitimate access while catching the recursive walk pattern. Cross-checked against The Hacker News' reporting that the directory is Anthropic Claude's artifact dir. Cross-checked against: • https://www.ox.security/blog/malware-slop-new-malicious-npm-package-leaks-its-own-github-private-token/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/malicious-npm-package-stole-files-from.html

[LLM] Node.js exfiltration to GitHub Contents API following /mnt/user-data read Command & Control Medium
Detects the exfiltration leg of mouse5212-super-formatter: a node/npm-spawned process making outbound HTTPS to api.github.com on a host that just read /mnt/user-data. Catches the GitHub Contents API PUT pattern even if the package is renamed, by correlating the file-read and the upload within a short window. Rationale: Targets the exact exfiltration channel from the OX Security writeup (GitHub Contents API call from a node-spawned process) and correlates it with the prior /mnt/user-data file walk within 10 minutes. The temporal join is what makes this article-specific — node hitting api.github.com alone is noisy (legitimate package installs do it constantly); pairing it with the Claude artifact-dir read is not. Confirmed by The Register's reporting on the GitHub-Contents-API exfil channel. Cross-checked against: • https://www.ox.security/blog/malware-slop-new-malicious-npm-package-leaks-its-own-github-private-token/ • https://www.theregister.com/cyber-crime/2026/05/27/supply-chain-brain-drain-npm-attacker-foolishly-leaks-own-github-private-token/5247424 • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/malicious-npm-package-stole-files-from.html

let Window = 10m;
let FileWalks = DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)

    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","npm","npx","yarn","pnpm","python","python3")

| where Timestamp between (FileReadStart .. FileReadStart + Window)
| project FileReadStart, NetTimestamp = Timestamp,

| order by FileReadStart desc
let Window = 10m;

              by DvcHostname, ActingProcessId, ActingProcessName, ActorUsername
    | where FilesRead >= 3;
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstHostname endswith "api.github.com" or Url has "api.github.com"

| order by FileReadStart desc

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession

            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"

    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"

   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] FortiClient fortitray.exe spawning cmd.exe to run .cmd script from EMS Trace\scripts path (CVE-2026-35616 EKZ dropper) Installation High
Hunts the unique dropper chain Arctic Wolf observed in CVE-2026-35616 exploitation: the legitimate FortiClient tray binary fortitray.exe being abused to launch a GUID-named .cmd file from C:\Program Files (x86)\Fortinet\FortiClient\logs\Trace\scripts\ (the EMS-managed script-deployment directory). This parent-child shape is the highest-fidelity host signal for this campaign and rarely appears in benign FortiClient operation. Rationale: Uses the article's exact dropper chain (fortitray.exe -> cmd.exe -> .cmd) plus the Arctic Wolf report's specific EMS deployment path FortiClient\logs\Trace\scripts\ which carries GUID-named .cmd payloads. Cross-checked the Arctic Wolf and Darktrace writeups, both of which name this exact path as IOC-grade. Cross-checked against: • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog-uk/forticlient-ems-exploited-cve-2026-35616-to-deliver-ekz-infostealer-disguised-as-a-fortinet-patch/ • https://www.darktrace.com/blog/forticlient-ems-exploited-inside-the-attack-chain-and-post-exploitation-tactics • https://cybersecuritynews.com/forticlient-code-execution-vulnerability/

| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\\[a-f0-9\-]{8,}\.cmd"
    or ProcessCommandLine has @"\logs\Trace\scripts\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,

| order by Timestamp desc

    or CommandLine has @"\logs\Trace\scripts\"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ProcessId
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: FortiClient fortitray.exe Spawning cmd.exe with .cmd Script from EMS Trace Path

description: Detects fortitray.exe spawning cmd.exe to execute a .cmd script from the FortiClient EMS-managed Trace\scripts directory - the dropper chain observed in CVE-2026-35616 / EKZ infostealer activity reported by Arctic Wolf in May 2026.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/threat-actors-exploit-critical.html

| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, CommandLine, ParentImageFileName], function=count())

[LLM] PowerShell HTTP POST to EKZ infostealer C2 83.138.53.110 Actions on Objectives High
Alerts on any outbound connection from powershell.exe / pwsh.exe to the hard-coded EKZ infostealer C2 IP 83.138.53.110. The article confirms the .cmd-launched encoded PowerShell wrapper is what performs exfiltration (the stealer itself has no network code), so any PowerShell-to-this-IP egress is high-fidelity intrusion evidence. Rationale: Article explicitly states the PowerShell wrapper (not the stealer binary) performs HTTP POST exfiltration to 83.138.53.110. Pinning the detection to process=powershell + IP=83.138.53.110 produces near-zero FPs. Corroborated by Arctic Wolf and Darktrace IOC lists. Cross-checked against: • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog-uk/forticlient-ems-exploited-cve-2026-35616-to-deliver-ekz-infostealer-disguised-as-a-fortinet-patch/ • https://www.darktrace.com/blog/forticlient-ems-exploited-inside-the-attack-chain-and-post-exploitation-tactics

[LLM] EKZ infostealer execution by FortiEndpoint_Patch.exe filename or known SHA256 Installation High
Hash- and name-based alert for the EKZ infostealer binary that Arctic Wolf reported being dropped under C:\ProgramData and other paths during CVE-2026-35616 exploitation. The article gives both the masquerading filename (FortiEndpoint_Patch.exe, posing as a Fortinet update) and five SHA256 hashes plus SHA1/MD5 — any of which firing is unambiguous post-compromise evidence. Rationale: Article-supplied IOCs: five SHA256, one SHA1, one MD5, and the masquerade filename FortiEndpoint_Patch.exe. Corroborating Arctic Wolf and Darktrace writeups also include the remote-hosted name p.exe. Hash hits are zero-FP intrusion evidence. Cross-checked against: • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog-uk/forticlient-ems-exploited-cve-2026-35616-to-deliver-ekz-infostealer-disguised-as-a-fortinet-patch/ • https://www.darktrace.com/blog/forticlient-ems-exploited-inside-the-attack-chain-and-post-exploitation-tactics • https://securityaffairs.com/192817/malware/cve-2026-35616-forticlient-ems-flaw-actively-exploited-in-malware-attacks.html
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1036.005 T1059.001

    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where FileName =~ "FortiEndpoint_Patch.exe" or FileName =~ "p.exe"
        or SHA256 in~ (EKZ_SHA256) or SHA1 in~ (EKZ_SHA1) or MD5 in~ (EKZ_MD5)

[LLM] Non-browser process accessing Chromium / Gecko credential stores in EKZ stealer pattern Actions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the EKZ credential-harvest behaviour: a non-browser, unsigned (or non-vendor-signed) process opening Chrome / Edge 'Login Data', 'Cookies', 'Web Data' or Firefox / Thunderbird / LibreWolf 'logins.json', 'key4.db', 'cookies.sqlite' followed by a write to C:\ProgramData. The article confirms the stealer writes its harvested loot to a ProgramData log file before the PowerShell wrapper exfiltrates it. Rationale: Article calls out both browser families (Chromium and Gecko) and the ProgramData staging location explicitly. Hunt is structured around the EKZ stealer's specific dual-fingerprint (browser-store read + ProgramData write) rather than the generic 'something touched Login Data' which is noisy. Cross-checked against: • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog-uk/forticlient-ems-exploited-cve-2026-35616-to-deliver-ekz-infostealer-disguised-as-a-fortinet-patch/ • https://www.darktrace.com/blog/forticlient-ems-exploited-inside-the-attack-chain-and-post-exploitation-tactics
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1539 T1074.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
let browser_artifacts = dynamic(["Login Data","Cookies","Web Data","logins.json","key4.db","cookies.sqlite","formhistory.sqlite","signons.sqlite","places.sqlite"]);
let browser_procs = dynamic(["chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe","firefox.exe","librewolf.exe","thunderbird.exe","opera.exe","vivaldi.exe","iexplore.exe"]);
let vendor_signed = dynamic(["Google LLC","Microsoft Corporation","Mozilla Corporation","Brave Software, Inc.","Opera Norway AS","Vivaldi Technologies"]);
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ (browser_artifacts) or FolderPath startswith @"C:\ProgramData\"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ (browser_procs)
| where InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName !in~ (vendor_signed)
| summarize ArtifactsTouched = make_set(FileName, 25),
            ArtifactCount = dcount(FileName),
            Folders = make_set(FolderPath, 10),
            FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
          by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName,
             InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| where ArtifactCount >= 2 or (ArtifactCount >= 1 and Folders has @"\ProgramData\")
| order by LastSeen desc
let browser_artifacts = dynamic(["Login Data","Cookies","Web Data","logins.json","key4.db","cookies.sqlite","formhistory.sqlite","signons.sqlite","places.sqlite"]);
let browser_procs = dynamic(["chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe","firefox.exe","librewolf.exe","thunderbird.exe","opera.exe","vivaldi.exe","iexplore.exe"]);
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFileName in~ (browser_artifacts) or TargetFilePath startswith @"C:\ProgramData\"
| where ActingProcessName !endswith @"\chrome.exe"
     and ActingProcessName !endswith @"\msedge.exe"
     and ActingProcessName !endswith @"\firefox.exe"
     and ActingProcessName !endswith @"\brave.exe"
     and ActingProcessName !endswith @"\librewolf.exe"
     and ActingProcessName !endswith @"\thunderbird.exe"
     and ActingProcessName !endswith @"\opera.exe"
| summarize ArtifactsTouched = make_set(TargetFileName, 25),
            ArtifactCount = dcount(TargetFileName),
            Folders = make_set(TargetFilePath, 10),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
          by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName
| where ArtifactCount >= 2 or (ArtifactCount >= 1 and Folders has @"\ProgramData\")
| order by LastSeen desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @TargetFilename:(*\\"Login Data"* OR *\\Cookies OR *\\Web\ Data OR *\\logins.json OR *\\key4.db OR *\\cookies.sqlite OR *\\formhistory.sqlite OR *\\ProgramData\\*) -@Image:(*\\chrome.exe OR *\\msedge.exe OR *\\firefox.exe OR *\\brave.exe OR *\\librewolf.exe OR *\\thunderbird.exe OR *\\Chrome.exe OR *\\MsEdge.exe OR *\\Firefox.exe)
(#event_simpleName=FileWritten OR #event_simpleName=FileOpenInfo)
| regex("(?i)(Login Data|Cookies|Web Data|logins\\.json|key4\\.db|cookies\\.sqlite|formhistory\\.sqlite|ProgramData\\\\)", field=TargetFileName)
| NOT ContextImageFileName=/\\(chrome|msedge|firefox|brave|librewolf|thunderbird|opera|vivaldi)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
| count > 1

[LLM] EMS-pushed encoded PowerShell fan-out: identical fortitray-launched PS across many endpoints in short window Delivery High
Detects the article's signature lateral pattern — threat actors abusing FortiClient EMS as a malware-delivery channel — by hunting for the same Base64-encoded PowerShell command appearing across multiple managed endpoints within minutes, all parented by fortitray.exe -> cmd.exe. A single host running encoded PS is noise; the same encoded blob fanning out across the EMS fleet near-simultaneously is the unique CVE-2026-35616 abuse fingerprint. Rationale: Article's central claim is that EMS itself became the delivery channel: 'every managed endpoint became a potential execution target without requiring a separate intrusion path to each device'. Detecting the same encoded PowerShell across N hosts in T minutes, all rooted at fortitray.exe, is the unique signature — no generic encoded-PS rule covers this multi-host correlation. Verified against the Arctic Wolf and Darktrace IOC narratives. Cross-checked against: • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog-uk/forticlient-ems-exploited-cve-2026-35616-to-deliver-ekz-infostealer-disguised-as-a-fortinet-patch/ • https://www.darktrace.com/blog/forticlient-ems-exploited-inside-the-attack-chain-and-post-exploitation-tactics
ATT&CKT1072 T1059.001 T1027 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
let LookbackHours = 24h;
let WindowMinutes = 30m;
let FanoutHosts = 3;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackHours)
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "cmd.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName =~ "fortitray.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-EncodedCommand", "-enc ", "-ec ", " -e ")
| extend B64 = extract(@"(?i)-(?:e(?:nc(?:odedcommand)?)?)\s+([A-Za-z0-9+/=]{40,})", 1, ProcessCommandLine)
| where isnotempty(B64)
| summarize HostCount = dcount(DeviceId),
            Hosts = make_set(DeviceName, 50),
            Users = make_set(AccountName, 50),
            FirstSeen = min(Timestamp),
            LastSeen = max(Timestamp),
            SampleCmd = any(ProcessCommandLine),
            DecodedSample = base64_decode_tostring(any(B64))
          by B64
| where HostCount >= FanoutHosts
| where (LastSeen - FirstSeen) <= WindowMinutes
| order by HostCount desc, LastSeen desc
let LookbackHours = 24h;
let WindowMinutes = 30m;
let FanoutHosts = 3;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackHours)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\powershell.exe" or NewProcessName endswith @"\pwsh.exe"
| where ParentProcessName endswith @"\cmd.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("-EncodedCommand", "-enc ", "-ec ", " -e ")
| extend B64 = extract(@"(?i)-(?:e(?:nc(?:odedcommand)?)?)\s+([A-Za-z0-9+/=]{40,})", 1, CommandLine)
| where isnotempty(B64)
| join kind=leftouter (
    SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackHours)
    | where EventID == 4688
    | where NewProcessName endswith @"\cmd.exe"
    | where ParentProcessName endswith @"\fortitray.exe"
    | project CmdPID = NewProcessId, Computer, CmdStart = TimeGenerated
  ) on Computer
| where TimeGenerated between (CmdStart .. CmdStart + 5m)
| summarize HostCount = dcount(Computer),
            Hosts = make_set(Computer, 50),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            SampleCmd = any(CommandLine),
            DecodedSample = base64_decode_tostring(any(B64))
          by B64
| where HostCount >= FanoutHosts
| where (LastSeen - FirstSeen) <= WindowMinutes
| order by HostCount desc, LastSeen desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\\cmd.exe OR *\\CMD.EXE) @Image:(*\\powershell.exe OR *\\PowerShell.exe OR *\\POWERSHELL.EXE OR *\\pwsh.exe) @CommandLine:(*\-EncodedCommand* OR *\-enc\ * OR *\-ec\ *) @ParentCommandLine:(*fortitray* OR *FortiTray* OR *FORTITRAY*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\(powershell|pwsh)\.exe$/i ParentBaseFileName=/cmd\.exe$/i
| regex("(?i)-(e(nc(odedcommand)?)?|ec)\\s+[A-Za-z0-9+/=]{40,}", field=CommandLine)
| GrandparentImageFileName=/fortitray\.exe$/i OR regex("(?i)fortitray", field=ParentCommandLine)
| B64 := /(?i)-(?:e(?:nc(?:odedcommand)?)?)\s+(?<encoded>[A-Za-z0-9+\/=]{40,})/
| groupBy([encoded], function=[count(field=aid, distinct=true, as=HostCount), collect([ComputerName, CommandLine])])
| HostCount >= 3

ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-35616")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-35616")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc
