Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.execution
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'
    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:
    - DevOps tooling that legitimately uses encoded command for
      cross-shell escaping
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.

ClearFake Uses BSC Testnet Smart Contracts for Takedown-Resistant Command and Control

Cyber Security News
2026-05-28 18 use cases 10 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

A new and dangerously clever malware campaign called ClearFake has been caught using blockchain smart contracts to run its operations, making it nearly impossible for security teams to shut it down. Instead of relying on traditional servers that can be taken offline, the attackers hid their command-and-control infrastructure inside the BNB Smart Chain testnet, a [&#8230;] The post ClearFake Uses BSC Testnet Smart Contracts for Takedown-Resistant Command and Control appeared first on Cyber Security News .

Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] ClickFix Run-dialog rundll32 with WebDAV UNC port syntax · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — ClearFake Uses BSC Testnet Smart Contracts for Takedown-Resistant Command and Co

Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] ClearFake C2 query to BNB Smart Chain testnet RPC endpoint · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] ClearFake dllhost spawned by rundll32 injecting into Chrome/Edge · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
[LLM] ClearFake C2 query to BNB Smart Chain testnet RPC endpoint Command & Control High
Detects browser or any endpoint process performing a JSON-RPC query to bsc-testnet-rpc.publicnode.com — the Stage 1 ClearFake EtherHiding lookup that fetches the on-chain Stage 2 JavaScript from Smart Contract A before the ClickFix overlay renders. No legitimate enterprise application routinely contacts BSC testnet RPC. Rationale: Pivots on the single named RPC endpoint the article explicitly recommends blocking (bsc-testnet-rpc.publicnode.com) — the chain breaks here before any payload runs. Corroborated by Trend Micro vendor write-up (trendmicro.com/en_us/research/26/e/smart-contracts-for-command-and-control.html) and gbhackers coverage. Cross-checked against: • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/26/e/smart-contracts-for-command-and-control.html • https://gbhackers.com/clearfake-abuses-bsc-testnet/ • https://www.vmray.com/threat-intelligence-insights-pivoting-off-the-blockchain/
ATT&CKT1102.002 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has "bsc-testnet-rpc.publicnode.com"
   or (RemoteUrl has "publicnode.com" and RemoteUrl has "bsc-testnet")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName,
          User = InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DnsQuery has "bsc-testnet-rpc.publicnode.com"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName, EventProduct
| union (
    ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where HttpHostName has "bsc-testnet-rpc.publicnode.com" or Url has "bsc-testnet-rpc.publicnode.com"
    | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, Url, HttpHostName, EventProduct
)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] ClickFix Run-dialog rundll32 with WebDAV UNC port syntax Exploitation High
Detects rundll32.exe launched directly from explorer.exe (Run dialog paste) with a UNC path embedding the @80 / @443 WebDAV mini-redirector syntax — the exact ClickFix execution shape Trend Micro recorded for the ClearFake Windows payload that pulls put34b.camp into memory. Rationale: Combines three article-specific signals: parent explorer.exe (Run dialog), child rundll32.exe, and the exact WebDAV UNC `\\host@port\` syntax or literal put34b.camp filename. The triple combination has near-zero benign baseline; explorer→rundll32 alone is high-FP, the UNC port syntax disambiguates. Cross-checked with gbhackers ClickFix-WebDAV writeup and Trend Micro report. Cross-checked against: • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/26/e/smart-contracts-for-command-and-control.html • https://gbhackers.com/rundll32-and-webdav/ • https://www.cyberproof.com/blog/the-clickfix-evolution-new-variant-replaces-powershell-with-rundll32-and-webdav/
ATT&CKT1218.011 T1059 T1204.004 T1570
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "rundll32.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "explorer.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\\\\[^\\]+@(80|443|8080)\\"
   or ProcessCommandLine has "put34b.camp"
   or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\\\\[^\\]+@\d+\\.+,#1\b"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName,
          AccountName, AccountDomain,
          ProcessCommandLine,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\rundll32.exe"
| where ParentProcessName endswith @"\explorer.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\\\\[^\\]+@(80|443|8080)\\"
     or CommandLine has "put34b.camp"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Rundll32 loads put34b.camp DLL via WebDAV mini-redirector Installation High
Detects the actual in-memory load of the ClearFake stage payload — the file named put34b.camp loaded by rundll32.exe — and the WebClient (svchost) outbound HTTP fetch that retrieves it. Fires even if the Run-dialog parent chain is obscured. Rationale: put34b.camp is a campaign-specific filename named verbatim in the article's IoC table, with no benign WebDAV use case. Combining DLL image-load by rundll32 + WebClient svchost fetch gives both the local effect and the wire-layer corroboration. Cross-referenced with Trend Micro and ASR/WebDAV reporting (lindensec.com). Cross-checked against: • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/26/e/smart-contracts-for-command-and-control.html • https://www.lindensec.com/post/dissecting-a-live-clickfix-attack-etherhiding-webdav-abuse-and-how-asr-saves-the-day
ATT&CKT1218.011 T1105 T1071.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
let LoadEvents = DeviceImageLoadEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where FileName =~ "put34b.camp" or FolderPath has "put34b.camp"
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
              InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessId;
let WebDavFetch = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "svchost.exe"
    | where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("WebClient","WebDav","DavSetCookie")
    | where RemotePort in (80, 443, 8080)
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort,
              InitiatingProcessCommandLine;
LoadEvents
| union WebDavFetch
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "put34b.camp" or TargetFilePath has "put34b.camp"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| union (
    ImNetworkSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where SrcUsername != "" and DstPortNumber in (80, 443, 8080)
    | where NetworkApplicationProtocol in~ ("http","https")
    | where Url has "put34b.camp" or DstHostname has "put34b.camp"
    | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcUsername, Url, DstHostname, DstIpAddr
)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] ClearFake dllhost spawned by rundll32 injecting into Chrome/Edge Actions on Objectives High
Detects the post-exploitation chain where rundll32.exe spawns dllhost.exe which then injects remote threads into chrome.exe and msedge.exe to harvest browser sessions, cookies, and saved credentials (SectopRAT / ACRStealer behaviour confirmed in Trend Micro execution profiles). Rationale: dllhost.exe legitimately runs only as a COM surrogate and always carries the `/Processid:{...}` GUID. A dllhost.exe without that switch and parented to rundll32.exe is highly anomalous — Trend Micro's execution profile (Figure 7) shows this exact tree leading to chrome.exe / msedge.exe credential theft. Excluding the legitimate CLSID-arg form keeps FPs low. Cross-checked against: • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/26/e/smart-contracts-for-command-and-control.html • https://blog.vega.io/posts/clickfix_sectoprat_campaign/
ATT&CKT1055.002 T1055.003 T1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
let SuspiciousDllHost = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "rundll32.exe"
    | where FileName =~ "dllhost.exe"
    | where ProcessCommandLine !has "/Processid:{"   // legitimate dllhost has COM CLSID
    | project DllHostTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, AccountName,
              DllHostPid = ProcessId, ParentPid = InitiatingProcessId,
              ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine;
let RemoteThreadInjection = DeviceEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where ActionType in ("CreateRemoteThreadApiCall","ProcessInjectionDetected","AsyncRpcThreadCreated")
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "dllhost.exe"
    | where FileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe","firefox.exe")
    | project InjectionTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName,
              InjectorPid = InitiatingProcessId, TargetProcess = FileName, ActionType;
SuspiciousDllHost
| join kind=inner RemoteThreadInjection on DeviceId
| where InjectionTime between (DllHostTime .. DllHostTime + 5m)
| project DllHostTime, InjectionTime, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentCmd, DllHostPid, TargetProcess, ActionType
| order by DllHostTime desc
let SuspiciousDllHost = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where ParentProcessName endswith @"\rundll32.exe"
    | where ActingProcessName endswith @"\dllhost.exe"
    | where ActingProcessCommandLine !has "/Processid:{"
    | project DllHostTime = TimeGenerated, DvcHostname,
              ActorUsername, ActingProcessId, ParentProcessCommandLine;
SuspiciousDllHost
source:windows.sysmon AND @EventID:1 AND @ParentImage:(*\\rundll32.exe OR *\\Rundll32.exe OR *\\RUNDLL32.EXE) AND @Image:(*\\dllhost.exe OR *\\Dllhost.exe OR *\\DLLHOST.EXE) AND -@CommandLine:"/Processid:{*"
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\dllhost\.exe$/i ParentBaseFileName=/rundll32\.exe/i
| NOT regex("/Processid:\\{", field=CommandLine)
| join({
    #event_simpleName=DllInjection TargetImageFileName=/(chrome|msedge|brave|firefox)\.exe$/i
    | groupBy([aid, ContextProcessId], function=count())
  }, field=[aid, TargetProcessId], include=[TargetImageFileName])
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, CommandLine, TargetImageFileName], function=[count(), min(@timestamp)])
ENDPOINT

| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name="rundll32.exe" Processes.process_name="dllhost.exe" by host Processes.user Processes.process Processes.parent_process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | join host [| tstats summariesonly=t count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="dllhost.exe" by host Processes.process_id | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | rename process_id as injector_pid] | eval reason="rundll32 -> dllhost (ClearFake browser-injection chain)" | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name="rundll32.exe" Processes.process_name="dllhost.exe" by host Processes.user Processes.process Processes.parent_process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | join host [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="dllhost.exe" by host Processes.process_id | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | rename process_id as injector_pid] | eval reason="rundll32 -> dllhost (ClearFake browser-injection chain)" | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
[LLM] ClearFake Python RAT staging in FileZilla Data masquerade directory Installation High
Detects dllhost.exe (or any non-FileZilla process) writing pythonw.exe / helper.py / libvlccore.dll / remote_debugging.pyd into a FileZilla Data subdirectory — the ClearFake masquerade location for the Python-based RAT and ACRStealer DLL sideload triad described in Trend Micro's Figure 8. Rationale: Four named filenames + FileZilla folder + a non-FileZilla writer is a near-zero baseline shape. The article calls the FileZilla Data directory out explicitly as the masquerade target (Figure 8), and libvlccore.dll is reused for the VLC DLL-sideload triad — both highly campaign-specific. Cross-checked with Vega.io ClickFix-SectopRAT analysis and Trend Micro report. Cross-checked against: • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/26/e/smart-contracts-for-command-and-control.html • https://blog.vega.io/posts/clickfix_sectoprat_campaign/
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1574.001 T1059.006 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("pythonw.exe","helper.py","libvlccore.dll","remote_debugging.pyd")
| where FolderPath has "FileZilla"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("FileZilla.exe","filezilla.exe","msiexec.exe","setup.exe","FileZilla_3*.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName,
          User = InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          DroppedFile = FileName,
          FolderPath,
          SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFileName in~ ("pythonw.exe","helper.py","libvlccore.dll","remote_debugging.pyd")
| where TargetFilePath has "FileZilla"
| where ActingProcessName !endswith @"\FileZilla.exe"
     and ActingProcessName !endswith @"\msiexec.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

description: Detects pythonw.exe, helper.py, libvlccore.dll or remote_debugging.pyd being written into a FileZilla directory by a process that is not the legitimate FileZilla installer/binary - the ClearFake ACRStealer / SectopRAT masquerade pattern.
references:

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("MetaMask.exe","Exodus.exe","Atomic.exe","electrum.exe","Bitcoin.exe","Phantom.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Ethereum\keystore\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Bitcoin\wallet.dat"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Exodus\exodus.wallet*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Electrum\wallets\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\MetaMask\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Phantom\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Atomic\Local Storage\*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("MetaMask.exe","Exodus.exe","Atomic.exe","electrum.exe","Bitcoin.exe","Phantom.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT

| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email

    [| tstats `summariesonly` count

          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count

    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")

The Gentlemen ransomware: Dissecting a self-propagating Go encryptor

Microsoft Security Blog
2026-05-28 16 use cases 11 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Microsoft Threat Intelligence presents a comprehensive analysis of The Gentlemen, a Go-based ransomware deployed by affiliates of Storm-2697 that combines per-file ephemeral key encryption with an aggressive self-propagation module to deploy itself across an entire network using series of simultaneous lateral movement techniques per target. The post The Gentlemen ransomware: Dissecting a self-propagating Go encryptor appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog .

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] The Gentlemen ransomware known SHA256 file/process sightings · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] The Gentlemen ransomware command-line argument signature · [LLM] The Gentlemen ransomware --full dual child relaunch (--system + --shares) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — The Gentlemen ransomware: Dissecting a self-propagating Go encryptor
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Gentlemen ransomware SYSTEM elevation via gentlemen_system scheduled task · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
[LLM] Gentlemen ransomware SYSTEM elevation via gentlemen_system scheduled task Installation High
Detects The Gentlemen ransomware's privilege-escalation sequence: it deletes any existing scheduled task named gentlemen_system, then creates a new one-time task running its binary under NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM and triggers it. The literal task name is a strong unique-string signal. Rationale: gentlemen_system is the literal, hardcoded scheduled-task name documented in the Microsoft analysis of Storm-2697's encryptor; combined with schtasks.exe parent it is article-specific and not a generic schtasks alert. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1053/005/
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1548
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "gentlemen_system"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/create", "/delete", "/run")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, AccountDomain,
          ParentProcess = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\schtasks.exe"
| where CommandLine has "gentlemen_system"
| where CommandLine has_any ("/create", "/delete", "/run")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account = SubjectUserName, Domain = SubjectDomainName,
          ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] The Gentlemen ransomware known SHA256 file/process sightings Delivery High
Direct IOC sweep across file-write and process-execution telemetry for the three SHA256 hashes attributed to The Gentlemen encryptor by Microsoft Threat Intelligence. Highest-fidelity signal available for the campaign. Rationale: These three SHA256 values are the article's hard IOCs for The Gentlemen encryptor and the literal hashes Microsoft uses in its own Defender XDR hunting query (Code Block 1). Fixed Sentinel column choices: ImFileEvent has only TargetFileSHA256, ImProcessCreate uses Computer/DvcHostname, CommonSecurityLog uses DeviceHostName. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/05/28/the-gentlemen-ransomware-dissecting-a-self-propagating-go-encryptor/
ATT&CKT1486

(DeviceEvents

[LLM] The Gentlemen ransomware command-line argument signature Exploitation High
Hunts for processes invoked with the unique combination of command-line flags exposed by Storm-2697's Gentlemen encryptor (--password, --full, --system, --shares, --spread, --ultrafast, --superfast). These flags are documented in the author's own usage banner and are atypical for legitimate Go binaries. Rationale: These flag names come straight from the article's documented usage prompt for the binary (Figure 2, Table 1). The combination of --password + any of {full,spread,shares,system,ultrafast,superfast} is essentially never seen on legitimate software because The Gentlemen invents its own argument grammar. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/05/28/the-gentlemen-ransomware-dissecting-a-self-propagating-go-encryptor/
ATT&CKT1059 T1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--password"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--full", "--spread", "--shares", "--system", "--ultrafast", "--superfast", "--silent", "--wipe", "--keep")
| extend FlagCount = countof(ProcessCommandLine, "--")
| where FlagCount >= 2
| extend BadPasswordMatch = ProcessCommandLine has "9VoAvR7G"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine,
          ParentFile = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256, BadPasswordMatch
| order by BadPasswordMatch desc, Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has "--password"

[LLM] The Gentlemen ransomware --full dual child relaunch (--system + --shares) Exploitation High
Detects the ransomware's documented --full operating mode where the parent binary spawns two children of itself: one with --system (local volume encryption under a SYSTEM scheduled task) and one with --shares (mapped network drives / UNC encryption in the user session). The same image hash appearing as both parent and two children within seconds is a high-fidelity execution-tree signature. Rationale: The article documents this exact behaviour: `--full` mode causes the binary to spawn two children of itself, one appended with `--system` (encrypts local drives via scheduled task) and one with `--shares` (encrypts UNC/mapped drives in user session). The dual-child same-PPID shape on a single host is an article-specific TTP not present in generic ransomware rules. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/05/28/the-gentlemen-ransomware-dissecting-a-self-propagating-go-encryptor/
ATT&CKT1106 T1486 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
let lookback = 7d;
let children = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
    | where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--system", "--shares")
    | where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "--full"
    | extend Mode = case(ProcessCommandLine has "--system", "system",
                          ProcessCommandLine has "--shares", "shares",
                          "other")
    | project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName,
              ParentSHA256 = InitiatingProcessSHA256,
              ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
              ChildSHA256 = SHA256,
              ChildFile = FileName,
              ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
              Mode, InitiatingProcessId;
children
| summarize Modes = make_set(Mode),
            FirstTime = min(Timestamp),
            LastTime = max(Timestamp),
            ChildCmds = make_set(ChildCmd, 5),
            ChildHashes = make_set(ChildSHA256, 5)
            by DeviceId, DeviceName, ParentSHA256, ParentCmd, InitiatingProcessId
| where array_length(Modes) >= 2
| order by FirstTime desc
let lookback = 7d;
let children = SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
    | where EventID == 4688

                          CommandLine has "--shares", "shares",

let parents = SecurityEvent

    | where CommandLine has "--full"
    | project ParentTime = TimeGenerated, Computer, ParentPid = NewProcessId,
              ParentImage = NewProcessName, ParentCmd = CommandLine;
children
| join kind=inner parents on Computer, $left.ProcessId == $right.ParentPid

          ChildImage = NewProcessName, ChildCmd = CommandLine, Mode, Account = SubjectUserName

            ChildCmds = make_set(ChildCmd, 5)
            by Computer, ParentImage, ParentCmd, Account
| where array_length(Modes) >= 2

source:(windows.security OR windows.sysmon) (@EventID:4688 OR @EventID:1) @ParentCommandLine:*--full* @CommandLine:(*--system* OR *--shares*)

| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentPid], function={ collect([CommandLine]) | count(as=cnt) })

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")

ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT

| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "078163d5c16f64caa5a14784323fd51451b8c831c73396b967b4e35e6879937b", "fe1033335a045c696c900d435119d210361966e2fb5cd1ba3382608cfa2c8e68") or SHA1 in~ ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "078163d5c16f64caa5a14784323fd51451b8c831c73396b967b4e35e6879937b", "fe1033335a045c696c900d435119d210361966e2fb5cd1ba3382608cfa2c8e68") or MD5 in~ ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "078163d5c16f64caa5a14784323fd51451b8c831c73396b967b4e35e6879937b", "fe1033335a045c696c900d435119d210361966e2fb5cd1ba3382608cfa2c8e68")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "078163d5c16f64caa5a14784323fd51451b8c831c73396b967b4e35e6879937b", "fe1033335a045c696c900d435119d210361966e2fb5cd1ba3382608cfa2c8e68") or SHA1 in~ ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "078163d5c16f64caa5a14784323fd51451b8c831c73396b967b4e35e6879937b", "fe1033335a045c696c900d435119d210361966e2fb5cd1ba3382608cfa2c8e68") or MD5 in~ ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "078163d5c16f64caa5a14784323fd51451b8c831c73396b967b4e35e6879937b", "fe1033335a045c696c900d435119d210361966e2fb5cd1ba3382608cfa2c8e68")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "078163d5c16f64caa5a14784323fd51451b8c831c73396b967b4e35e6879937b", "fe1033335a045c696c900d435119d210361966e2fb5cd1ba3382608cfa2c8e68"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

status: experimental

[LLM] Gogs RCE: git rebase invoked with --exec flag (argument injection) Exploitation High
Detects the Gogs zero-day argument-injection RCE in flight: the Gogs server process invokes 'git rebase' with an attacker-controlled branch name that smuggles a '--exec=' flag, causing arbitrary command execution as the Gogs user. The smoking gun is a 'git rebase' process whose command line contains '--exec' (or '-x') and whose parent is the gogs binary. Rationale: The article explicitly names the injected flag ('--exec') and the abused command path ('git rebase' during 'Rebase before merging'), with the Gogs server as the parent that invokes git. A 'git rebase' process whose parent is gogs and whose argv contains '--exec' has effectively no legitimate use — the Gogs codebase never legitimately passes --exec to rebase. Cross-referenced with Rapid7's earlier Gogs argument-injection family (CVE-2024-39930/39932/39933) which the article explicitly compares this flaw to. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sonarsource.com/blog/securing-developer-tools-unpatched-code-vulnerabilities-in-gogs-1 • https://www.sonarsource.com/blog/securing-developer-tools-unpatched-code-vulnerabilities-in-gogs-2 • https://thehackernews.com/2024/07/critical-vulnerabilities-disclosed-in.html • https://github.com/gogs/gogs/issues/7777
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004 T1068
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "gogs"
| where FileName =~ "git"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "rebase"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--exec", "-x=", "--exec=")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          GogsCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          GitCmd  = ProcessCommandLine,
          GitPath = FolderPath,
          ProcessId
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName endswith "/gogs" or ParentProcessName =~ "gogs"
| where ActingProcessName endswith "/git" or ActingProcessName =~ "git"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "rebase"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("--exec", "-x=", "--exec=")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          GogsCmd = ParentProcessCommandLine,
          GitCmd  = ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Post-exploit shell or LOLBin spawned by git invoked from Gogs server Installation High
Follow-on detection for the Gogs --exec argument injection: once 'git rebase --exec=<cmd>' fires, git executes the attacker's command, producing a process tree of gogs -> git -> /bin/sh|bash|curl|wget|nc|python. Hunts for any non-git child of a git process whose parent is the Gogs server binary — the post-exploitation footprint the article describes ('compromise the server, dump credentials, pivot'). Rationale: The article enumerates the post-exploit objectives explicitly — 'compromise the server, read every repository on the instance, dump credentials (password hashes, API tokens, SSH keys, 2FA secrets), pivot to other network-accessible systems'. Git itself has zero legitimate reason to spawn shells, network tools, or interpreters; in the Gogs server context, git only invokes other git plumbing binaries. Any non-git child of git on a Gogs host is the --exec payload landing. Confirmed pattern matches Rapid7's documented Gogs argument-injection family (CVE-2024-39930/39932/39933). Cross-checked against: • https://www.sonarsource.com/blog/securing-developer-tools-unpatched-code-vulnerabilities-in-gogs-1 • https://thehackernews.com/2024/07/critical-vulnerabilities-disclosed-in.html • https://www.darkreading.com/vulnerabilities-threats/attackers-exploited-gogs-zero-day-months
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1505.003 T1552.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
let GogsHosts = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "gogs" and FileName =~ "git"
    | distinct DeviceId;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where DeviceId in (GogsHosts)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "git"
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName =~ "gogs"
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","curl","wget","nc","ncat","python","python3","perl","socat","base64","chmod","id","whoami","uname","cat","openssl")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ChildProc = FileName,
          ChildCmd  = ProcessCommandLine,
          GitCmd    = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          GogsCmd   = InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName endswith "/git" or ParentProcessName =~ "git"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","curl","wget","nc","ncat","python","python3","perl","socat","base64","chmod","id","whoami","uname","cat")
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has "rebase" or ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("--exec","-x=")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          ChildProc = ActingProcessName,
          ChildCmd  = ActingProcessCommandLine,
          GitCmd    = ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.executable.path:(*/bin/sh OR */bin/bash OR */bin/dash OR */curl OR */wget OR */nc OR */ncat OR */python OR */python3 OR */perl OR */socat OR */base64 OR */whoami OR */id) @process.ppid:* -@process.executable.path:(*/snapd/* OR */apt/* OR */dpkg/*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/^git$/i
| ImageFileName=/\/(sh|bash|dash|zsh|curl|wget|nc|ncat|python3?|perl|socat|base64|chmod|id|whoami|uname|cat|openssl)$/i
| join(query={#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/^gogs$/i ImageFileName=/\/git$/i}, field=aid, include=[aid, ComputerName])
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())

// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-8110", "CVE-2024-55947", "CVE-2024-39933", "CVE-2024-39932", "CVE-2026-26194", "CVE-2024-39930")

| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-8110", "CVE-2024-55947", "CVE-2024-39933", "CVE-2024-39932", "CVE-2026-26194", "CVE-2024-39930")

ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("d8fcd57a71f9f6e55b063939dc7c1523660b7383", "efda81e1100ea977321d0f2eeb0dfa7a6b132abd") or SHA1 in~ ("d8fcd57a71f9f6e55b063939dc7c1523660b7383", "efda81e1100ea977321d0f2eeb0dfa7a6b132abd") or MD5 in~ ("d8fcd57a71f9f6e55b063939dc7c1523660b7383", "efda81e1100ea977321d0f2eeb0dfa7a6b132abd")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("d8fcd57a71f9f6e55b063939dc7c1523660b7383", "efda81e1100ea977321d0f2eeb0dfa7a6b132abd") or SHA1 in~ ("d8fcd57a71f9f6e55b063939dc7c1523660b7383", "efda81e1100ea977321d0f2eeb0dfa7a6b132abd") or MD5 in~ ("d8fcd57a71f9f6e55b063939dc7c1523660b7383", "efda81e1100ea977321d0f2eeb0dfa7a6b132abd")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["d8fcd57a71f9f6e55b063939dc7c1523660b7383", "efda81e1100ea977321d0f2eeb0dfa7a6b132abd"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-33825", "CVE-2026-41091", "CVE-2026-45498", "CVE-2026-45585")

| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-33825", "CVE-2026-41091", "CVE-2026-45498", "CVE-2026-45585")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time

| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07

            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime

      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")

OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Shai-Hulud worm GitHub Action workflow file dropped under .github/workflows · [LLM] npm/yarn/pnpm postinstall hook spawning credential-harvest tooling · Suspicious browser extension installation · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Cyberhaven trojanized Chrome extension C2 callback to cyberhavenext.pro · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Mini Shai-Hulud npm worm exfil to filev2.getsession.org · [LLM] postmark-mcp BCC exfil to giftshop.club · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
[LLM] Cyberhaven trojanized Chrome extension C2 callback to cyberhavenext.pro Command & Control High
Hunts for DNS/HTTPS resolution to cyberhavenext.pro from Chromium-based browsers — the C2 domain used by the malicious Cyberhaven Chrome extension (v24.10.4, active 25–26 Dec 2024) and ~35 related extensions in the Secure Annex cluster. The extension's worker.js fetched its config from this host before exfiltrating cookies and authenticated sessions. Rationale: Article names cyberhavenext.pro as an explicit IOC. Cross-checked against Cyberhaven's own engineering blog, Secure Annex's cluster analysis, Darktrace and Obsidian Security write-ups — all confirm the domain as the C2 used by the malicious worker.js bundled in extension v24.10.4 to retrieve config before stealing cookies/auth sessions. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cyberhaven.com/engineering-blog/cyberhavens-preliminary-analysis-of-the-recent-malicious-chrome-extension • https://secureannex.com/blog/cyberhaven-extension-compromise/ • https://www.darktrace.com/blog/cyberhaven-supply-chain-attack-exploiting-browser-extensions • https://www.obsidiansecurity.com/resource/behind-the-breach-malicious-attack-on-cyberhavens-chrome-extension-developer-team
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1176 T1539
